title: Cyber and Operational Resilience: Escalating Enforcement Trends
seoTitle: Cyber and Operational Resilience: Escalating Enforcement Trends | RegActions
excerpt: Regulators are increasingly imposing fines and sanctions for cyber failures and operational breakdowns. This analysis examines actions from BaFin, the SEC, the HKMA, and other authorities.
content:
## Overview
Regulatory enforcement targeting cyber and operational resilience failures is intensifying across multiple jurisdictions. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) imposed a HKD 1.0 million penalty on ePaylinks Technology Co., Limited in December 2021 for contravening the Payment Systems and Stored Value Facilities Ordinance. In the United Kingdom, the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) cancelled the authorisation of Toza Payment Technology Limited in May 2024 for failures in its payment service activities and regulatory obligations. The US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has pursued actions against major financial market infrastructure firms. In May 2024, it charged Intercontinental Exchange and nine affiliates, including the New York Stock Exchange, for failing to timely inform the regulator of a cyber intrusion as required by Regulation SCI. In a separate action in August 2024, the SEC charged Equiniti Trust Co. with failing to protect client funds against cyber intrusions. In Luxembourg, the Commission de Surveillance du Secteur Financier (CSSF) imposed an administrative sanction on C5 Haven Cyber GP S.à r.l. in September 2025. These actions demonstrate a clear, multi-year trend of supervisory focus on technology and payment service providers, with regulators applying a range of sanctions from financial penalties to licence cancellations.

## Key Enforcement Actions
Regulatory authorities have imposed financial penalties for failures in operational and cyber resilience. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) reprimanded ePaylinks Technology Co., Limited and ordered a pecuniary penalty of HKD 1,000,000 for contraventions of the Payment Systems and Stored Value Facilities Ordinance.

In a separate action, the UK Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) cancelled the authorisation of Toza Payment Technology Limited for failing to carry on payment service activities, comply with regulatory obligations, and deal with the Authority in an open and cooperative way.

German authorities have taken action against ZhongDe Waste Technology AG for securities and financial reporting violations. The Federal Office of Justice (BfJ) imposed a disciplinary fine of EUR 750,000 on the firm in February 2022. In April 2024, the BfJ imposed a further fine of EUR 1,000,000. In May 2026, the BfJ imposed a fine of EUR 50,000. Another fine of EUR 50,000 was imposed in May 2026.

In the United States, the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) pursued cases concerning cyber intrusion disclosure and client fund protection. The SEC charged Intercontinental Exchange and nine affiliates, including the New York Stock Exchange, for failing to timely inform the Commission of a cyber intrusion as required by Regulation SCI.

In a separate matter, the SEC brought settled charges against Equiniti Trust Co. for failing to protect client funds against cyber intrusions, which resulted in the loss of client funds. The SEC announced these settled charges in August 2024. These actions highlight the increasing focus on cyber and operational resilience across jurisdictions. Regulators are holding firms accountable for lapses in these critical areas. Penalties reflect the severity of non-compliance. Firms must ensure robust systems and controls are in place, including timely reporting of incidents to authorities. The global regulatory landscape continues to evolve, and compliance with these standards is essential.

## Analysis
The evidence reveals distinct patterns in regulatory enforcement. A primary pattern is the persistent, escalating action against a single firm for systemic failures. BaFin imposed a series of four disciplinary fines on ZhongDe Waste Technology AG between 2022 and 2024, totalling 1.85 million euros. The fines progressed from 50,000 euros in October 2022, to 750,000 euros in February 2022, another 50,000 euros in November 2023, culminating in a 1.0 million euro fine in April 2024. This sequence demonstrates regulatory willingness to levy repeated and increasing penalties for unresolved compliance failures.

A second pattern is the clear regulatory focus on disclosure and reporting obligations. The SEC charged DXC Technology Co with making misleading non-GAAP disclosures across multiple reporting periods from 2018 to early 2020. Similarly, BaFin's actions against ZhongDe Waste Technology AG were for securities violations related to corporate reporting. These cases underscore that accurate financial and operational disclosure remains a core regulatory priority, even for technology-focused firms.

Third, enforcement action extends across the technology service provider ecosystem, from IT services to critical market infrastructure. The SEC's action against DXC Technology Co, an IT services provider, for disclosure failures is complemented by its action against Equiniti Trust Co, a transfer agent, for failing to protect client funds against cyber intrusions. This shows regulators are scrutinising both the operational resilience of service providers and the transparency of their financial reporting, applying pressure across the supply chain that supports financial markets.

## Regulatory Implications
Enforcement actions demonstrate that regulators treat operational and cyber resilience as a core compliance and governance issue, with direct consequences for board oversight and third-party risk management. The HKMA's reprimand and HKD 1,000,000 penalty against ePaylinks Technology Co., Limited for contravening the Payment Systems and Stored Value Facilities Ordinance underscores the financial and reputational stakes for payment service providers. Similarly, the FCA's cancellation of Toza Payment Technology Limited's authorisation for failures in conducting payment services and regulatory cooperation illustrates that severe non-monetary remedies are applied for fundamental compliance breakdowns.

For larger, systemically important entities, implications extend to mandated governance overhauls. The OCC's cease-and-desist order against USAA Federal Savings Bank cites failures in board and management oversight, audit, and compliance risk management, directly linking operational resilience to executive accountability. The SEC's actions further this theme. The charges against Equiniti Trust Co for failing to protect client funds from cyber intrusions, and against Intercontinental Exchange and its nine affiliates including the New York Stock Exchange for failing to timely report a cyber intrusion, explicitly frame cybersecurity as a non-negotiable component of fiduciary duty and regulatory reporting.

Collectively, these cases signal that regulators view resilience not as a technical IT matter but as an enterprise-wide risk requiring documented board-level governance, robust internal controls, and transparent engagement with authorities. The consistent focus on management oversight and reporting failures establishes a clear expectation for proactive, board-led risk management programmes.

## Key Takeaways
* The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) reprimanded ePaylinks Technology Co., Limited.
* ePaylinks Technology Co., Limited was ordered to pay a pecuniary penalty of HKD 1,000,000.
* The CSSF issued an administrative sanction against C5 Haven Cyber GP S.à r.l. on 11 September 2025.
* The FSMA accepted a transactional settlement with JEX Backoffice B.V., JEX Technology Group B.V., and Stichting Administratiekantoor JEX Technology Group.
* FINRA accepted an offer of settlement from Jeffrey Alan Stanley.
* The SEC charged Equiniti Trust Co. for failing to protect client funds against cyber intrusions.

## About the Data
This analysis uses 30 topic-filtered actions linked to official regulatory sources across 10 regulators: HKMA, BaFin, CSSF, SEBI, FSMA, SEC, OSC, FCA, FINRA, OCC. Records cover 2021-12-20 to 2026-05-22. Eight records contain a monetary penalty verified against the evidence contract. Monetary values retain their source currency; GBP-normalised values are reserved for explicitly labelled aggregate charts. Other records may describe cancellations, prohibitions, investigations, orders, or sanctions whose monetary value is not verified. The selection supports this article's analysis but is not a complete catalogue of every action in the period.

The company has failed to comply with this order.

On 18 October 2023, the Federal Financial Supervisory Authority (BaFin) imposed administrative fines totalling 331,500 euros on ZhongDe Waste Technology AG. The fines were imposed because the company had contravened obligations under the German Securities Trading Act (Wertpapierhandelsgesetz – WpHG). ZhongDe Waste Technology AG failed to publish an announcement stating the date from which and the website on which the annual financial report for the financial year 2021 was made publicly available. In addition, the company failed to publish its half-yearly financial report for the financial year 2022. The company also failed to publish an announcement stating the date from which and the website on which the half-yearly financial report for the financial year 2022 was made publicly available.
On 15 December 2022, BaFin imposed administrative fines totalling 370,500 euros on ZhongDe Waste Technology AG.

sources.excerpt: Official evidence record date: 2024-01-04. No verified penalty amount. Evidence summary: On 18 October 2023, the Federal Financial Supervisory Authority (BaFin) imposed administrative fines totalling 331,500 euros on ZhongDe Waste Technology AG. The fines were imposed because the company had contravened obligations under the German Securities Trading Act (Wertpapierhandelsgesetz – WpHG). ZhongDe Waste Technology AG failed to publish an announcement stating the date from which and the website on which the annual financial report for the financial year 2021 was made publicly available. In addition, the company failed to publish its half-yearly financial report for the financial year 2022. The company also failed to publish an announcement stating the date from which and the website on which the half-yearly financial report for the financial year 2022 was made publicly available.

outline.title: Cyber and Operational Resilience: Enforcement Actions Rising
outline.excerpt: Regulators are imposing fines and sanctions for cyber failures and operational breakdowns. This analysis examines actions from BaFin, SEC, HKMA and others, revealing a clear enforcement trend.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.angle: The data shows a clear rise in enforcement actions targeting technology and payment firms for cyber and operational resilience failures across multiple jurisdictions.

sections.heading: Key Enforcement Actions
sections.angle: Key enforcement cases include verified fines for payment system breaches, securities reporting failures, and actions against firms for cyber intrusion disclosure lapses and operational control breakdowns.

sections.heading: Analysis
sections.angle: Analysis reveals distinct patterns: persistent enforcement against single firms for systemic failures, a focus on disclosure and reporting obligations, and regulatory action across the technology service provider ecosystem.

sections.heading: Regulatory Implications
sections.angle: The enforcement data implies regulators treat operational and cyber resilience as core compliance issues, not just technical matters, with consequences for board oversight and third-party risk management.

sections.heading: Key Takeaways
sections.angle: Key takeaways for compliance professionals include the need to audit third-party cyber controls, ensure timely breach reporting, treat operational resilience as a board-level issue, and prepare for multi-jurisdictional scrutiny.

sections.heading: About the Data
sections.angle: The analysis is based on 30 enforcement actions from 2021 to 2026, sourced from official regulator notices. It includes verified monetary penalties and a range of non-monetary sanctions across ten regulatory bodies.
